title: Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Amendment (Near-new Dwelling Interests) Bill 2019
short_title: Foreign Acquisitions and Takeovers Fees Imposition Amendment (Near-new Dwelling Interests) Bill 2019

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would impose reconciliation fees on developers selling near-new dwellings to foreign purchasers under exemption certificates, alongside a companion housing bill governing collection.
The fee framework would apply from 1 July 2017, covering dwellings whose earlier sale contracts failed to settle and which were subsequently sold under those certificates.
Developers holding certificates before enactment would receive a transitional first payment period ending at the first reporting date at least 30 days after commencement.
changes: The fees imposition law would gain provisions imposing the amount payable for near-new dwelling sales.
Its fee section heading and explanatory references would be updated to accommodate the new charging category.
A fee would cover each relevant sale within the transitional reconciliation period.
summary.affected: Property developers selling homes under near-new dwelling exemption certificates would be affected.

speeches.speaker: Jim Chalmers
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the bills but argued they are insufficient, noting that home ownership has dropped to its lowest level since the 1960s, house prices in major cities have risen over 15% in five years, household debt is at a record 200% of income, and over one million low-income households face housing stress. They also criticised the government for lacking a comprehensive plan, citing stagnant wages as a deliberate policy design and warning that low interest rates risk inflating asset prices without improving affordability.

speeches.speaker: Adam Bandt
speeches.brief: Young people face housing unaffordability because house prices have risen from six times a graduate's income decades ago to over 12 times now, while wages are low and government tax subsidies treat housing as an investment rather than a basic right; no Australian city is affordable to rent on Newstart.
